items.text: A Wisp of Wind
Therapy Room, The Foundation

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Sorry, Ms. Klara.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: You may have lost control of your arcane skill because of the trauma you've experienced. I should have focused on this in previous sessions; I missed it.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: So, for the immediate future, we should keep you away from any mirrors or reflective surfaces until you overcome this disorder.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Do you agree?
The room has nothing but a pair of chairs and a table with a desk lamp. They sit across from one another.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: Yes, miss, uh, Doctor.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Alright. Let me explain the treatment plan the Foundation has created for you.
The psychiatrist keenly identifies that Kakania's mind has started to wander.
She taps the writing board with her pen.
Kakania looks up and blinks.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: Hmm?

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: Oh, my mind wandered again? Sorry.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: What's on your mind this time?
Kakania glances around the room, her eyes eventually falling on the dim, yellow lamp.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: Nothing. It's just this room reminds me of somewhere.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: I've been in one similar to this before. Back in Vienna.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: What were you doing there?

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: I was going to meet a friend.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: A friend, it seemed that I never really knew.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Would you like to talk about this friend?

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: Sorry, I don't know where to start.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: It's okay. Let's get back to our topic, then.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: I'm sure you've noticed, Ms. Klara, that I've never stopped you from consciously or unconsciously recalling traumatic memories, as you did just now.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: This is the initial stage of our treatment. We guide the patient to trace back their traumatic experiences in order to identify any causes and triggers of their disorder.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Then, through controlled exposure to these triggers, we start the process of desensitization, with the final goal being to help the patient create positive coping strategies to deal with these triggers.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: This treatment, it's quite different from the therapeutic strategies I'm familiar with.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: In what way?

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: For me, pushing patients to relive their traumatic memories is never good.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: And recalling trauma too frequently would only serve to damage the patient's psyche further—even exacerbate the isolation of these traumas in their mind.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: While free talk—and the more difficult conversations that stem from it—can be a useful tool to build trust, focusing only on trauma won't benefit anyone.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: So you prioritize psychoanalysis. I see.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Remember the first time we met? You expressed your disagreement with the session arrangement.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: I still think that a weekly session is too infrequent for sustained psychological observation.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: I understand, and as I've explained before, psychology has moved far beyond the exploratory stage of the early 20th century that you're familiar with.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Psychoanalytic therapy—"talk therapy," if you will—has seen many advancements throughout the century.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: To be more specific, Laplace's psychotherapeutic method has long been separated from Freud's. Many of his theories have been proven wrong.
This is not her era anymore. It has never been clearer than now.
She clenches her fist, and a sharp pain shoots from her palm. She looks down to see a blood-soaked shard clutched in her hand.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: This ...

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: Hmm?

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: What are you looking at, Ms. Klara?

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Ms. Klara?

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: I—

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: I'm hallucinating.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Thank you for telling me. What do you see?

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: A fragment of a mirror.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: As I said, my mirror broke, and I haven't been able to use my arcane skill since.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Yes, the report stated that your arcane skill is related to mirrors—that they serve as a kind of "wand" for you. But it didn't tell me this.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: What is it that you can do with a mirror?

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: My arcane skill is "Vingler's Mirror." It allows me to see what people are thinking.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: You can understand it as reflecting people's inner desires into the mirror.
The psychiatrist takes a moment to contemplate this.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: I see. This is how you treat your patients. So now, during our conversation, you fear I'm "prying" into you.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Because now you think that's what you did to your patients.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: You no longer consider that treatment the right way of helping people, do you?

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: During our treatment, I'd like you to shift your understanding of yourself. You're not a psychiatrist in our sessions, Ms. Klara.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: You're a patient who needs treatment.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: To be honest, you're not the first psychiatrist I've treated. There are a lot of people at headquarters who have been traumatized by the "Storm," including some of my colleagues.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: How are they now?

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Before I answer, I want to ask you a question. Have you heard about this theory:

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: "Growth is the process of behavior reinforcement."

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: This sounds like behaviorism.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: I thought you'd recognize it. Well, our method could be seen as a distant, less extreme evolution of behaviorism.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: It's called "recognition reappraisal." We work with patients to identify and reframe the negative emotions they hold toward a particular traumatic event. Eventually, as they learn to better recognize and manage their emotions, the trauma will feel less overwhelming than it once did.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: And to answer your question, most of my colleagues were able to modify their emotional response to the events that traumatized them through this process.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: A small number of them are still under treatment because they haven't been able to reframe the negative emotions associated with their trauma.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Their friends didn't make it to the safe zone. Seeing the hands reaching out to them, the melted painting-like faces ... It keeps haunting them.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Much like how it haunts you, doesn't it?
Speechless, Kakania looks down again, opening and clenching her fist repeatedly.
There's nothing in it.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: You unconsciously replay the events in Vienna before the "Storm" over and over in your head. And you keep mentioning that mirror. You relive those negative emotions again and again but are unable to reframe them—to understand them differently.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: I'll need some more information in order to help you in this process.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: What do you need to know?

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: You identify yourself as a psychiatrist, and, outdated though it may be, you have a strong knowledge of psychoanalysis, yet you still use your arcane skill to treat your patients.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: It sounds counterintuitive to me.
Kakania furrows her brow.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: You're right. It is counterintuitive for a psychiatrist.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: My arcane skill is one of my therapies. But there are many others I employ. All based on Dr. Freud's theories.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: I treat my patients with science. This arcanum is just a kind of parlor trick.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: I see. A fusion therapy using an arcane skill and following Freudian theories could have some lasting value.

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: I wonder, have you ever used this on yourself?

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: What do you mean?

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: I mean, have you looked at yourself in your own mirror?

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: I'm sure I must have, but—

items.speaker: Psychiatrist
items.text: Yes or no?

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: It's not possible. I—

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: "Your first hand mirror is for reflecting yourself. Your first table mirror is for observing others."

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: Every Vingler knows this.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: I had a hand mirror, so I must—

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: I must have ...

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: Have I?

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: Have I looked at myself in my own mirror?
